h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: The L2 gradient scales as alpha/batch and is applied n/b times per epoch, so raising alpha at tiny batches drives weight collapse far more than at large batches.
Function change per Adam step grows with fan-in, so wider nets destabilize more at learning rates of 0.08-1 and gain less from width there.
At very high learning rates, larger batches reduce gradient noise and the number of chaotic updates, stabilizing otherwise divergent training.
Large batches leave few updates per epoch, so a higher learning rate compensates for the lost step count.
Large-step errors compound through three ReLU layers, causing dead units and divergence at lower learning rates than in shallow nets.
The L2 penalty shrinks every weight matrix, and the product of shrunken matrices collapses signal multiplicatively in deeper nets.
Extra penalty compounds across three layers of shrunken weights, so increasing alpha costs deep nets more than single-layer nets.
Stacking narrow 16-40 unit ReLU layers creates information bottlenecks and dead-unit cascades, so extra depth hurts there.
With one hidden layer, width is the only source of capacity, so widening helps most there.
Large batches give few updates, and wider nets make more function-space progress per step, so width offsets the reduced step budget.
